fields.problem:
Title: Number of $k^p \bmod q$ classes when $q\%p > 1$

I want to show that when $p, q$ are primes, $k^p\bmod q$ takes on $q-1$ distinct values (as $k$ ranges over positive integers) if and only if $q \not\equiv 1 \pmod p$.  (It is easy to verify this computationally for small primes, eg $p I can show the "only if" part easily (but crudely) [Update: and incorrectly, as noted in Jyrki Lahtonen's comment]
for $q>4$ via Euler's theorem by noting that $4^j-1$
is never prime if $j>1$, so that $q \equiv 1 \pmod p[U+000D CONTROL]
\implies q>p \implies \exists k>1$ such that 
$\phi(q) = q-1 = k\cdot p$, hence (taking $x=4^k$)
we have $\exists x\not\equiv 1$ such that
$x^p=4^{k\cdot p}=4^{q-1}\equiv 1$, which ensures
that $|S(p,q)| For the "if" part I've been trying to apply Lagrange's theorem for a group with operation $\circ$ with $a\circ b \equiv a^p\cdot b^p\bmod q$ which is easy to show is closed and associative with identity and inverse, but have been going in circles on this part.

What is a better approach for proving the "only if" part?  What's a better direction for the "if" part?
fields.source_context:
0001 | First we give a number-theoretic proof for the direction you did not deal with. After that, we give a couple of proofs for the other direction. These are  similar to the proof that you described, but fill the gap mentioned in the comment by @Jyrki Lahtonen. 
0002 | 
0003 | As much as possible, your notation is used. The primality of $p$ is nowhere used, and is not needed. I do not think that assuming primality allows for any real simplification. 
0004 | 
0005 | Suppose that $q \not \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, and $a^p \equiv b^p \pmod{q}$. We will show that $a\equiv b \pmod{q}$.  We can assume that neither $a$ nor $b$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $q$.  
0006 | 
0007 | Since $q\not\equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, the numbers $q-1$ and $p$ are relatively prime.  By Bezout's Theorem  there exist integers $m$, $n$ such that $m(q-1)+np=1$.  Thus 
0008 | $$a=a^1=a^{m(q-1)+np}=a^{(q-1)m}a^{pn}\qquad\qquad\text{(Equation $1$)}$$
0009 | By Fermat's Theorem, $a^{(q-1)m} \equiv 1\pmod{q}$.
0010 | From Equation $1$, we conclude that 
0011 | $$a\equiv (a^p)^n \pmod{q}.$$
0012 | Similarly,
0013 | $$b \equiv (b^p)^n \pmod{q}.$$
0014 | 
0015 | It follows that if $a^p \equiv b^p \pmod{q}$ then $a \equiv b \pmod{q}$.
